questions.q: Sustained level turn constraint T_SL/W_TO = (β/α)[qC_D0/(βW/S) + Kn²β(W/S)/q]. Raising the required n moves its bucket:
questions.a: Up by a factor n, and to lower W/S by 1/n
w: Down by a factor n, and to higher W/S by n
Straight up by n², at the same W/S
Up by a factor n², and to higher W/S by n
questions.x: The bucket sits at βW/S = (q/n)√(C_D0/K) with minimum T_SL/W_TO = (β/α)·2n√(KC_D0), so it rises with n and moves to lower wing loading.

questions.q: With drag and rolling friction neglected, the simplified takeoff constraint T_SL/W_TO versus W_TO/S is:
questions.a: A straight line through the origin
w: A vertical line at the stall wing loading
A horizontal line set by the climb gradient
A bucket curve with a minimum at max L/D
questions.x: Mattingly's simple form T_SL/W_TO = (β²/α)·k_TO²(W_TO/S)/(s_TO ρ g C_Lmax) is linear in W_TO/S through the origin, with slope falling as field length, density and C_Lmax grow.

questions.q: At fixed altitude, as flight Mach rises from 0 to 0.8, which jet engine's thrust lapse α falls the most?
questions.a: High bypass turbofan, from its low specific thrust
w: Turbojet, from its high exhaust velocity and core flow
Afterburning turbojet, from its high T_t7
Low bypass turbofan, from its mixed exhaust
questions.x: Thrust is ṁ(V_e − V_0), and a high bypass engine has V_e close to V_0, so rising ram drag cuts its thrust fastest; turbojets hold α better with Mach, and a propeller's thrust falls roughly as P/V.

questions.q: Warmup and takeoff weight fraction 0.97, climb fraction 0.985. What is β = W/W_TO at the start of cruise? Give 3 decimals.
questions.x: β is the product of the preceding segment fractions: 0.97 × 0.985 = 0.955, and β keeps falling along the mission as fuel burns.

questions.q: Climb constraint with α = β = 1: q = 10,000 Pa, W/S = 4000 Pa, C_D0 = 0.02, K = 0.1, climb gradient (1/V)dh/dt = 0.1. Find T/W to 2 decimals.
Complete the sustained turn constraint
questions.a: n²
w: n
1/n²
√n
questions.x: Induced drag scales with C_L² and C_L = nβW_TO/(qS), so the induced term carries n².

questions.q: On Mars, with ρ about 1/70 of Earth's sea-level value, the stall constraint at fixed stall speed and C_Lmax:
questions.a: Moves left, to about 1/70 the allowed W/S
w: Moves right, to about 70 times the allowed W/S
Moves left, to about 1/√70 the allowed W/S
Stays fixed, since W/S already includes gravity
questions.x: The stall line is W/S = ½ρV_s²C_Lmax, so it scales directly with density and Mars aircraft need very low wing loading.

questions.q: Match each constraint to its shape on the T_SL/W_TO vs W_TO/S diagram
pairs: Straight line rising from the origin
Bucket, parasite term rising at low W/S
questions.x: Stall and landing depend on W/S alone, takeoff is linear in W/S, speed constraints form buckets from parasite and induced terms, and climb adds a P_s term.

questions.q: The service ceiling is the altitude where:
questions.a: Maximum rate of climb falls to 100 ft/min
w: Maximum rate of climb falls to zero
Maximum rate of climb falls to 1000 ft/min
Cruise Mach reaches the drag divergence Mach
questions.x: Service ceiling is where the best rate of climb is 100 ft/min (0.5 m/s); absolute ceiling is where it reaches zero and P_A just touches P_R.

questions.q: Compared with a piston prop, a jet's power available P_A versus airspeed:
questions.a: Grows about linearly, since P_A = TV with T nearly flat
w: Stays about flat, since prop shaft power is nearly constant
Falls as 1/V, since ram drag cuts the thrust
Grows as V³, matching the parasite power curve
questions.x: A jet's thrust is roughly constant with speed so P_A = TV rises linearly, while a prop delivers nearly constant power η_p P_shaft; rate of climb is (P_A − P_R)/W.

questions.q: In a steady unpowered glide, the maximum ground distance from height h in still air is:
questions.a: h·(L/D)_max, independent of weight
w: h·(L/D)_max, growing with √W
h·(L/D)_max², independent of weight
h/(L/D)_max, independent of weight
questions.x: tan γ = D/L, so the flattest glide is at (L/D)_max and distance = h·(L/D)_max; weight sets the best glide speed, which scales with √(W/S).

questions.q: An aircraft with (L/D)_max = 15 loses power at 3000 m above flat terrain in still air. Maximum glide distance, in km?
questions.x: Glide ratio equals L/D, so distance = h·(L/D)_max = 3000 m × 15 = 45 km.

questions.q: Prop Breguet range: η_p = 0.8, c = 8×10⁻⁷ 1/m (N of fuel per J of shaft work), L/D = 15, W_i/W_f = 1.25. Range in km (nearest 10)?
Complete the jet Breguet endurance equation (TSFC c, weight basis)
questions.a: L/D
w: V·L/D
D/L
questions.x: Jet endurance depends on L/D alone, so it peaks at (L/D)_max, independent of speed.

questions.q: Landing ground roll from touchdown speed V_TD with mean deceleration ā is about:
questions.a: s = V_TD²/(2ā)
w: s = V_TD²/(2ā) + V_TD/ā
s = V_TD²/ā
s = 2V_TD²/ā
questions.x: Constant deceleration from V_TD to rest gives s = V_TD²/(2ā); brakes, spoilers and reverse thrust shorten the roll by raising ā.

questions.q: Put the steps for finding absolute and service ceilings in order
steps: Compute P_R(V) at a chosen altitude from the drag polar
Compute P_A(V) at that altitude with the engine lapse
Find maximum rate of climb = max (P_A − P_R)/W
Repeat over altitudes and plot max rate of climb vs h
Read the ceilings at 0 and 100 ft/min
questions.x: Excess power over weight gives rate of climb at each altitude, and extrapolating the curve gives absolute (zero) and service (100 ft/min) ceilings.

questions.q: For a positively cambered wing, the negative stall curve on a V-n diagram is shallower than the positive one because:
questions.a: |C_L| at negative stall is smaller than C_Lmax
w: Negative gusts are weaker than positive gusts
The negative limit load is larger in magnitude
Dynamic pressure is lower in inverted flight
questions.x: The negative boundary is n = ρV²S C_L,neg/(2W), and camber makes |C_L,neg| smaller than C_Lmax, so it reaches its limit load at a higher speed.

questions.q: On a transport V-n diagram, the flaps-extended envelope differs from the clean one by:
questions.a: A +2.0 limit load and a speed cap at V_F
w: A +3.8 limit load and a speed cap at V_D
A +2.5 limit load and a speed cap at V_A
A −1.0 limit load and a speed cap at V_C
questions.x: With flaps extended, FAR 25 sets the positive maneuver limit at +2.0 up to the flap design speed V_F, while higher C_Lmax moves the stall curve left.

questions.q: Match each design speed to its meaning
pairs: 1 g stall speed in the configuration
Design speed for maximum gust intensity
Design dive speed closing the envelope
questions.x: V_S1 starts the envelope, V_F bounds the flap envelope, V_B sits where the stall curve meets the V_B gust line, and V_D closes the envelope on the right.

questions.q: W/S = 3000 Pa, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, C_Lmax = 1.5, positive limit load 3.8. Find the corner speed V_A in m/s.
Gust: ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³, U_de = 15 m/s, V_e = 150 m/s, a = 5.0 /rad, K_g = 0.8, W/S = 5000 Pa. Total load factor n = 1 + Δn? (2 decimals)
Complete the gust load increment (EAS form)
questions.text: Δn = ρ₀ U_de V_e a K_g / (2 ___)
questions.a: W/S
w: W
S
(W/S)²
questions.x: Gust load increment scales with lift slope and EAS and inversely with wing loading.

questions.q: Which aircraft is most likely to have gust loads, rather than maneuver loads, set its V-n envelope?
questions.a: Sailplane: low W/S, high AR, high lift slope
w: Fighter: high W/S, low AR, low lift slope
Aerobatic: high limit load factor near +6
Bizjet: high W/S, swept wing, low lift slope
questions.x: Δn grows with lift slope a and scales as 1/(W/S), so light, high aspect ratio aircraft see gust lines rise above the maneuver limit loads.

questions.q: Under FAR 25, the aircraft must be free of flutter up to:
questions.a: 1.15 V_D, a 15% margin beyond the dive speed
w: V_C, the design cruise speed at the cruise altitude
V_A, the design maneuvering speed
1.5 V_D, the ultimate speed margin
questions.x: Flutter clearance extends 15% beyond V_D/M_D, so the flutter boundary sits outside the right edge of the V-n envelope.

questions.q: At fixed T_t4 and overall pressure ratio, raising turbofan bypass ratio:
questions.a: Lowers specific thrust and lowers TSFC
w: Raises specific thrust and lowers TSFC
Lowers specific thrust and raises TSFC
Raises specific thrust and raises TSFC
questions.x: More bypass spreads the core energy over more air at lower jet velocity, so thrust per unit airflow drops while propulsive efficiency and TSFC improve.

questions.q: On a T-s diagram, a real (non-isentropic) compressor at the same pressure ratio reaches:
questions.a: Higher T_t3 and higher entropy than the ideal
w: Lower T_t3 and higher entropy than the ideal compressor
Higher T_t3 at the same entropy as the ideal
Lower T_t3 and lower entropy than the ideal
questions.x: Losses generate entropy, so the compression line slants right and ends on the same isobar at a higher temperature, needing more work.

questions.q: Compressor: T_t2 = 288 K, π_c = 20, γ = 1.4, isentropic efficiency η_c = 0.85. Find T_t3 in K.
Ideal ramjet thermal efficiency at M₀ = 3, γ = 1.4? Give 3 decimals.
questions.x: Ram compression gives τ_r = 1 + 0.2·9 = 2.8, and η_th = 1 − 1/τ_r = 0.643, rising with flight Mach.

questions.q: Complete the turbine isentropic efficiency
questions.a: h_t5s
w: h_t3
h_t5
h_t2
questions.x: Turbine efficiency is actual work over ideal work, with h_t5s the isentropic exit enthalpy at the same exit pressure.

questions.q: On a T-s diagram, afterburner heat addition appears as:
questions.a: Heating along a low pressure isobar after the turbine
w: Heating along the high pressure burner isobar, before the turbine
Isentropic expansion through the turbine
Heating at constant volume ahead of the nozzle
questions.x: The afterburner adds heat at the low pressure behind the turbine, giving a large rise in T and jet velocity with low cycle efficiency and high TSFC.

questions.q: Above about Mach 5 to 6, designers switch from ramjet to scramjet because:
questions.a: Subsonic diffusion gives huge T and shock losses
w: Supersonic flow cuts the residence time to zero
Ramjets need a compressor above Mach 5
Combustor pressure drops below ambient at Mach 5
questions.x: Slowing the flow to subsonic at high Mach drives static temperature toward dissociation and causes large stagnation pressure loss, so the scramjet burns in supersonic flow.

questions.q: Match each engine to its typical best flight Mach range
questions.x: Propulsive efficiency favors large mass flow at low speed, while ram compression takes over at high Mach.

questions.q: Complete the Biot-Savart result for a semi-infinite straight vortex
questions.text: At distance r abeam its end: w = Γ/(___ r)
questions.a: 4π
w: 2π
π
8π
questions.x: A semi-infinite filament induces half of the infinite vortex value Γ/(2πr), giving Γ/(4πr).

questions.q: Helmholtz's vortex theorems state that a vortex filament:
questions.a: Keeps constant strength and ends only at boundaries
w: Grows in strength along its length as it trails downstream
Decays in strength at a rate set by viscosity
Ends in the fluid wherever the lift goes to zero
questions.x: A vortex filament has constant strength along its length and extends to infinity, closes on itself, or ends on a boundary, which is why a lifting line sheds trailing vortices.

questions.q: Thin airfoil a₀ = 2π /rad, finite wing AR = 8, e = 0.9. Find the wing lift slope a = a₀/(1 + a₀/(πeAR)) in /rad.
An unswept airfoil has M_crit = 0.70. Using simple sweep theory, estimate M_crit at 30° sweep (2 decimals).
questions.x: The normal Mach component M cos Λ governs, so M_crit ≈ 0.70/cos 30° = 0.81.

questions.q: Flying within about one span of the ground, a wing experiences:
questions.a: Less downwash: lower induced drag, more lift at α
w: More downwash: higher induced drag, less lift at α
Less downwash: higher induced drag, less lift at α
More downwash: lower induced drag, more lift at α
questions.x: The ground acts like an image vortex system that reduces downwash, cutting induced drag and raising lift slope, which causes floating on landing.

questions.q: Whitcomb's transonic area rule says wave drag is minimized by:
questions.a: A smooth total cross-section area along x
w: A constant wing thickness ratio along the entire span
A fuselage with constant diameter along x
Maximum wing sweep at a given span and thickness
questions.x: Wave drag depends on the axial distribution of total cross-sectional area, so the fuselage is waisted at the wing (coke bottle) toward a Sears-Haack shape.

questions.q: In Raymer's estimate e = 1.78(1 − 0.045AR^0.68) − 0.64, raising AR from 6 to 10:
questions.a: Lowers e slightly, but K = 1/(πeAR) still falls
w: Raises e sharply, so K falls faster than 1/AR itself
Lowers e so much that K = 1/(πeAR) rises
Leaves e and K both unchanged at this level
questions.x: e drops from about 0.87 to 0.76 while πeAR grows from 16.4 to 23.8, so the induced drag factor K still falls with aspect ratio.

questions.q: Put the Prandtl lifting line solution steps in order
steps: Model the wing as a bound vortex Γ(y) shedding a trailing sheet dΓ/dy
Set α_eff = α − w/V at each section
Impose Γ = ½V c a₀(α_eff − α_L0) and solve, e.g. by Fourier series
questions.x: Each section sees the freestream reduced by downwash from the trailing sheet, and enforcing 2D section lift at α_eff gives the integro-differential equation for Γ(y).

questions.q: In forward flight at speed V, the advancing and retreating blade tip speeds are:
questions.a: ΩR + V and ΩR − V
w: ΩR + V/2 and ΩR − V/2
ΩR and ΩR − 2V
ΩR + 2V and ΩR − V
questions.x: At ψ = 90° the tip sees ΩR + V and at ψ = 270° it sees ΩR − V, with advance ratio μ = V/(ΩR).

questions.q: ΩR = 210 m/s, forward speed 80 m/s, speed of sound 340 m/s. Advancing tip Mach number (2 decimals)?
questions.x: M_tip,adv = (ΩR + V)/a = 290/340 = 0.85, near the onset of drag rise and noise.

questions.q: Retreating blade stall at high advance ratio happens because:
questions.a: Low local speed forces high α to hold roll balance
w: High local speed raises the drag on that side
Reversed flow on the advancing side drops its lift
Higher inflow on the retreating side lowers its α
questions.x: Lift on the retreating side must match the advancing side, and the lower relative speed there demands high blade pitch and α, which reaches stall first at the outboard sections.

questions.q: In a steady autorotation after engine failure, the rotor is driven by:
questions.a: Upflow through the disk, as height is traded for energy
w: Stored rotor inertia alone, decaying steadily to the ground
Tail rotor thrust fed back through the gearbox
Downflow through the disk from forward speed
questions.x: In descent, air flows up through the disk and the inner blade region produces a driving force that sustains rotor speed; the pilot flares to trade rotor energy for a soft landing.

questions.q: Ingenuity's 1.2 m coaxial rotors turn at about 2500 rpm mainly because:
questions.a: Thin air needs high ΩR for thrust, capped by tip Mach
w: Low gravity needs high ΩR to stabilize the craft
Dust storms demand high rpm for blade cleaning
Cold air raises the speed of sound, so high rpm is free
questions.x: Thrust scales with ρA(ΩR)², so Mars's low density demands high tip speed, while the low Martian speed of sound limits ΩR through compressibility.

questions.q: A Mars rotor of 0.6 m radius turns at 2500 rpm; local speed of sound is 240 m/s. Hover tip Mach number (2 decimals)?
Complete the blade element thrust per blade (small inflow angle)
questions.a: C_l
w: C_d
C_m
C_l²
questions.x: Each blade element produces sectional lift ½ρU²cC_l dr with U ≈ Ωr in hover, and integrating along the blades gives rotor thrust.

questions.q: Match each rotorcraft configuration to how it handles main rotor torque
pairs: Tail rotor thrust on a moment arm
Two counter-rotating rotors on one axis
Circulation control boom plus a direct jet
questions.x: Counter-rotating layouts cancel torque between the two rotors and spend no power on an anti-torque rotor, while single-rotor designs use a tail rotor or air jet for yaw balance.

questions.q: W_crew + W_payload = 10,000 lb, W_e/W_0 = 0.55, W_f/W_0 = 0.30. Find W_0 in lb.
Segment fractions: takeoff 0.97, climb 0.985, cruise 0.85, loiter 0.95, landing 0.995. With 6% reserve and trapped fuel, W_f/W_0 (3 decimals)?
In Raymer's W_f/W_0 = 1.06(1 − W_x/W_0), the factor 1.06 accounts for:
questions.a: About 6% reserve and trapped fuel
w: About 6% engine installation losses
About 6% empty weight growth margin
About 6% payload growth allowance
questions.x: The 6% allowance covers reserve fuel and trapped or unusable fuel on top of the mission fuel.

questions.q: Why are warmup, taxi, takeoff and landing weight fractions taken from historical data rather than Breguet?
questions.a: Short segments fit historical ratios best
w: Breguet applies only at supersonic speed
These segments burn no fuel in practice
Historical ratios include the payload drop
questions.x: These segments are brief, with high power and varying speed, so typical ratios such as 0.970 and 0.995 capture them well.

questions.q: Why does adding 100 kg of payload raise W_0 by much more than 100 kg?
questions.a: Fuel and structure scale with W_0: a growth factor
w: Payload adds wetted area, which doubles the drag
Extra payload lowers L/D by the same fraction
The empty weight fraction rises in step with payload
questions.x: W_0 = W_payload/(1 − W_f/W_0 − W_e/W_0), so each kilogram of payload also carries its share of fuel and structure, often a factor of 3 to 10.

questions.q: Typical section: torsional stiffness K_θ, lift slope a, area S, aerodynamic center a distance e ahead of the elastic axis. Divergence dynamic pressure is:
questions.a: q_D = K_θ/(e a S)
w: q_D = e a S/K_θ
q_D = K_θ/(e² a S)
q_D = K_θ a/(e S)
questions.x: Divergence occurs when the aerodynamic twisting stiffness q e a S equals K_θ, so stiffer sections and a smaller offset e raise q_D.

questions.q: Complete Raymer's loiter weight fraction (jet, TSFC c)
questions.a: (L/D)
w: (V·L/D)
(D/L)
questions.x: Loiter time E with constant L/D and c gives W_f/W_i = exp(−Ec/(L/D)), best at (L/D)_max for a jet.

questions.q: Match each mission segment to its typical Raymer weight fraction
questions.x: Short segments use historical ratios, while cruise and loiter come from the Breguet equations.

questions.q: Wind axes, thrust inclined α + ε to the velocity (ε = installed thrust angle). The tangential point-mass equation is:
questions.a: m dV/dt = T cos(α+ε) − D − W sin γ
w: m dV/dt = T cos(α+ε) − D + W sin γ
m dV/dt = T sin(α+ε) − D − W cos γ
m dV/dt = T cos(α+ε) − D − W cos γ
questions.x: Along the velocity vector, the thrust component T cos(α+ε) accelerates the aircraft while drag and the weight component W sin γ along the climbing path decelerate it.

questions.q: With bank angle φ = 0, the normal (vertical plane) equation becomes:
questions.a: mV dγ/dt = L + T sin(α+ε) − W cos γ
w: mV dγ/dt = L + T cos(α+ε) − W sin γ
mV dγ/dt = L − T sin(α+ε) − W cos γ
m dγ/dt = L + T sin(α+ε) − W cos γ
questions.x: Normal to the path, lift plus the thrust normal component minus W cos γ supplies the centripetal force mV dγ/dt.

questions.q: In the heading equation mV cos γ dψ/dt = (L + T sin(α+ε)) sin φ, the aircraft turns because:
questions.a: Banking tilts lift and normal thrust into the horizontal
w: Rudder side force pushes the nose toward the inside of the turn
Drag acts asymmetrically on the two wing halves
Gravity gains a component toward the turn centre
questions.x: The horizontal component of the normal aerodynamic and thrust force, (L + T sin(α+ε)) sin φ, provides the centripetal force that changes heading ψ.

questions.q: Steady, level, wings-level flight with small α + ε reduces the point-mass EOM to:
questions.a: T = D and L = W
w: T = W and L = D
T = D + W and L = W
T = D and L = W + D
questions.x: With dV/dt = 0, γ = 0, φ = 0 and cos(α+ε) ≈ 1, sin(α+ε) ≈ 0, thrust balances drag and lift balances weight.

questions.q: Level coordinated turn at V = 150 m/s and φ = 60°, g = 9.81 m/s². Turn rate in deg/s (2 decimals)?
Pull-up at the bottom of a vertical arc: V = 200 m/s, R = 1000 m, g = 9.81 m/s². Load factor n (2 decimals)?
questions.x: At the bottom, L − W = mV²/R, so n = 1 + V²/(gR) = 1 + 40000/9810 = 5.08.

questions.q: In a steady climb with small α + ε, the climb angle satisfies:
questions.a: sin γ = (T − D)/W
w: sin γ = (T − D)/L
tan γ = (T − D)/W
cos γ = (T − D)/W
questions.x: The tangential equation with dV/dt = 0 gives sin γ = (T − D)/W, and rate of climb V sin γ = (T − D)V/W.

questions.q: With n = L/W, thrust normal component neglected and φ = 0, the flight path angle rate is:
questions.a: dγ/dt = (g/V)(n − cos γ)
w: dγ/dt = (g/V)(n − sin γ)
dγ/dt = (V/g)(n − cos γ)
dγ/dt = (g/V)(n + cos γ)
questions.x: Dividing mV dγ/dt = L − W cos γ by mV gives dγ/dt = (g/V)(n − cos γ), so n = cos γ holds the path straight.

questions.q: At the bottom of an outside loop (aircraft inverted, centre above), the load factor is:
w: n = V²/(gR) − 1
n = 1 − V²/(gR)
questions.x: Inverted at the bottom, the aerodynamic force must hold weight and supply the centripetal force while pointing toward the aircraft's belly, giving the most negative load factor of the maneuver.

questions.q: Complete the energy height definition
questions.a: 2g
w: g
4g
questions.x: Energy height is total mechanical energy per unit weight: potential h plus kinetic V²/(2g).

questions.q: h = 10,000 m, V = 300 m/s, g = 9.81 m/s². Energy height h_e in m (nearest 10)?
Complete the specific excess power
questions.a: W
w: m
L
D
questions.x: Specific excess power is excess power per unit weight, with units of velocity, and equals dh_e/dt.

questions.q: Physically, specific excess power P_s = dh_e/dt measures:
questions.a: The rate at which the aircraft can climb, speed up, or both
w: The maximum sustained load factor available at a given speed
The fuel burned per unit of energy height gained
The thrust margin at the absolute ceiling
questions.x: P_s = dh/dt + (V/g)dV/dt, so excess power can be spent on climb rate, acceleration, or a mix of the two.

questions.q: Which EOM, multiplied by V/W, gives the energy equation behind Mattingly's master equation?
questions.a: Tangential, with dh/dt = V sin γ
w: Normal, with dγ/dt = g(n − cos γ)/V
Heading, with dψ/dt = g tan φ/V
Pitch moment, with dq/dt = M/I_yy
questions.x: Multiplying m dV/dt = T − D − W sin γ by V/W and using V sin γ = dh/dt gives (T − D)V/W = dh/dt + (V/g)dV/dt = dh_e/dt.

questions.q: Put the steps of the level turn derivation in order
steps: Set γ = 0 and dγ/dt = 0 in the normal equation
Get L cos φ = W, so n = 1/cos φ
Use the heading equation: L sin φ = mV dψ/dt
Combine for ω = dψ/dt = g√(n² − 1)/V and R = V/ω
questions.x: Vertical balance fixes n through bank angle, and the horizontal lift component sets turn rate and radius.

questions.q: Match each maneuver to its load factor (n = L/W, speed V, radius R)
questions.x: In each case the net of lift and the weight component along the radius, taken toward the centre, supplies the centripetal force mV²/R.

questions.q: Raymer's component buildup for parasite drag is:
questions.a: C_D0 = Σ(C_f FF Q S_wet)/S_ref + C_D,misc + C_D,L&P
w: C_D0 = Σ(C_f FF Q S_ref)/S_wet + C_D,misc + C_D,L&P
C_D0 = Σ(C_f FF Q)·S_wet·S_ref + C_D,misc
C_D0 = Σ(C_f + FF + Q)S_wet/S_ref + C_D,L&P
questions.x: Each component contributes skin friction times form factor times interference factor times its wetted area, normalized by the reference area, plus miscellaneous and leakage and protuberance terms.

questions.q: Complete the average laminar flat plate skin friction (Blasius)
questions.x: The Blasius solution gives average laminar C_f = 1.328/√Re over a plate of length l, with Re based on l.

questions.q: Turbulent flat plate: C_f = 0.455/(log₁₀Re)^2.58. Find C_f at Re = 10⁷ (4 decimals).
At the same Reynolds number, turbulent skin friction exceeds laminar because:
questions.a: A fuller velocity profile gives a steeper wall gradient
w: A thinner boundary layer lowers the momentum flux at the wall
Laminar flow separates earlier and adds pressure drag
Turbulent flow has a lower wall shear but larger area
questions.x: Turbulent mixing brings high momentum fluid close to the wall, so ∂u/∂y at the wall and the wall shear stress τ_w = μ ∂u/∂y are larger.

questions.q: In the component buildup, the form factor FF accounts for:
questions.a: Pressure drag and supervelocity from thickness
w: Drag rise where two components join at their junction
Drag of gaps, rivets and antennas
Lift-dependent drag at the cruise C_L
questions.x: FF scales flat plate friction up for a body with thickness, which raises local velocity and adds viscous pressure drag; it grows with t/c and with lower fineness ratio.

questions.q: An interference factor Q = 1.5 for a nacelle mounted close to a wing means:
questions.a: Its parasite drag is 50% above the isolated value
w: Its wetted area is 50% of the isolated component value
Its skin friction is 1.5 times the laminar value
Its form factor is 50% below the isolated value
questions.x: Q multiplies the component's isolated parasite drag to capture mutual flow interference at junctions; well faired parts have Q near 1.0.

questions.q: Equivalent skin friction C_fe = 0.003 and wetted area ratio S_wet/S_ref = 6. Estimate C_D0 (3 decimals).
questions.x: Raymer's quick estimate is C_D0 = C_fe·S_wet/S_ref = 0.003·6 = 0.018.

questions.q: Match each drag source to its cause
pairs: Shocks at transonic and supersonic speed
Tail force to trim, adding lift and induced drag
Momentum loss of engine cooling airflow
questions.x: These terms sit on top of skin friction and form drag in the full drag buildup.

questions.q: Which trailing edge device increases both camber and wing area, giving the largest ΔC_Lmax?
questions.a: Fowler flap
w: Plain flap
Split flap
Single slotted flap
questions.x: A Fowler flap translates aft and rotates, adding chord (area) and camber, and its slots re-energize the boundary layer over the flap.

questions.q: A leading edge slat mainly:
questions.a: Delays stall, extending the lift curve to higher α
w: Shifts α_L0 more negative at the same lift curve slope
Raises C_L at α = 0 through added camber
Lowers the lift slope to soften the stall
questions.x: The slat's high-energy slot flow eases the suction peak and adverse gradient on the main element, raising α_stall and C_Lmax along a nearly unchanged lift line.

questions.q: Deflecting a trailing edge flap changes the section lift curve by:
questions.a: Shifting α_L0 more negative, slope about the same
w: Raising α_stall, with α_L0 about the same
Doubling the lift slope, α_L0 about the same
Shifting α_L0 more positive, slope about the same
questions.x: Added camber moves the lift curve up and to the left, so C_L rises at each α while the stall angle falls slightly.

questions.q: Typical transport C_Lmax values, clean versus full landing configuration, are about:
questions.a: 1.5 clean and 2.8 landing
w: 0.8 clean and 1.2 landing
2.5 clean and 5.0 landing
1.5 clean and 1.6 landing
questions.x: Clean swept wings reach C_Lmax around 1.2 to 1.6, and multi-element slotted flaps with slats reach about 2.5 to 3.0.

questions.q: Without washout, a highly tapered wing tends to stall first:
questions.a: Near the tip, where local c_l peaks
w: At the root, where the chord is largest
Uniformly along the whole span
At mid-span, where the flap ends
questions.x: Taper loads the outboard sections to the highest local c_l, so washout (lower tip incidence) is added to make the root stall first and keep the ailerons effective.

questions.q: Landing: W/S = 5000 Pa, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, C_Lmax = 2.8. Stall speed in m/s?
Put the component drag buildup steps in order
steps: Compute each component's Re, capped by the surface roughness cutoff
Find C_f from the laminar and turbulent fractions
Apply form factor FF and interference factor Q
Sum C_f FF Q S_wet over components and divide by S_ref
Add miscellaneous, leakage and protuberance drag
questions.x: Reynolds number sets skin friction, FF and Q correct it for shape and installation, and the remaining small items complete C_D0.

questions.q: Complete the equivalent flat-plate area
questions.a: S_ref
w: S_wet
b²
c̄
questions.x: Equivalent flat-plate area is parasite drag divided by dynamic pressure, so f = C_D0 S_ref and D_0 = q f.

questions.q: For a statically stable aircraft to trim at positive α (nose-up C_m positive), it needs:
questions.a: C_mα < 0 and C_m0 > 0
w: C_mα > 0 and C_m0 > 0
C_mα < 0 and C_m0 < 0
C_mα > 0 and C_m0 < 0
questions.x: C_mα < 0 gives a restoring nose-down moment when α rises, and C_m0 > 0 places the trim point C_m = 0 at positive α.

questions.q: Complete the static margin
questions.a: c̄
w: b
l_t
x_np
questions.x: Static margin is the distance from the CG aft to the neutral point, in units of mean aerodynamic chord.

questions.q: x_np = 3.2 m, x_cg = 2.9 m (both measured aft from the same datum), c̄ = 2.0 m. Static margin as a fraction (2 decimals)?
questions.x: SM = (3.2 − 2.9)/2.0 = 0.15, i.e. 15% of the mean chord.

questions.q: l_t = 15 m, S_t = 20 m², c̄ = 4 m, S = 100 m². Horizontal tail volume coefficient V_H (2 decimals)?
questions.x: V_H = l_t S_t/(c̄ S) = 300/400 = 0.75, a typical tail volume for light general aviation aircraft; jet transports sit nearer 1.0.

questions.q: C_mα relates to static margin SM and lift slope C_Lα as:
questions.a: C_mα = −C_Lα·SM
w: C_mα = C_Lα·SM
C_mα = −C_Lα/SM
C_mα = −SM/C_Lα
questions.x: C_mα = C_Lα(x_cg − x_np)/c̄ = −C_Lα·SM, so a larger margin gives a stronger nose-down restoring moment.

questions.q: The stick-fixed neutral point is:
questions.a: The CG location where C_mα = 0
w: The point where the lift acts at zero α
The CG location where C_m0 = 0
The point where elevator power is zero
questions.x: With the CG at the neutral point the aircraft is neutrally stable; CG positions ahead of it give C_mα < 0.

questions.q: Moving the CG aft toward the neutral point:
questions.a: Lowers static margin and the elevator needed per g
w: Raises static margin and the elevator needed per g
Lowers static margin and raises the trim drag
Raises static margin and lowers the trim drag
questions.x: An aft CG shortens the restoring arm, so the aircraft needs less elevator to trim and to pull g, and also carries less tail download.

questions.q: Match each item to what it means or sets (standard body axes, β positive with wind from the right)
pairs: Elevator power to trim at high C_L
Dihedral effect: roll away from sideslip
questions.x: Control power bounds the forward CG and stability bounds the aft CG; positive C_nβ yaws the nose into the wind and negative C_lβ rolls the wing level.

questions.q: Which surface contributes most to positive C_nβ (directional stability)?
questions.a: Vertical tail aft of the CG
w: Fuselage nose ahead of the CG
Wing dihedral angle
Horizontal tail aft of the CG
questions.x: Sideslip gives the vertical tail an angle of attack, and its side force acting aft of the CG yaws the nose back into the relative wind.

questions.q: Which change makes C_lβ more negative (stronger dihedral effect)?
questions.a: Moving the wing from low to high on the fuselage
w: Adding anhedral to the wing
Moving the wing from high to low on the fuselage
Changing aft sweep to forward sweep
questions.x: Geometric dihedral, a high wing position, and aft sweep all strengthen the dihedral effect, rolling the aircraft away from the sideslip.

questions.q: Lanchester's phugoid approximation: period T = π√2·V/g. Find T in s for V = 100 m/s, g = 9.81 m/s².
questions.x: T = π·1.414·100/9.81 = 45.3 s, a long period that grows linearly with speed.

questions.q: The short period mode frequency rises mainly with:
questions.a: Larger −C_mα (more static margin) and dynamic pressure
w: Smaller −C_mα (less static margin) and dynamic pressure
Larger C_lβ and roll damping C_lp
Larger tail volume V_V and C_nβ
questions.x: The short period is a fast pitch and α oscillation at nearly constant speed, with ω² roughly proportional to q·(−C_mα) plus pitch damping terms.

questions.q: Strong dihedral effect relative to directional stability tends to:
questions.a: Stabilize spiral but degrade Dutch roll damping
w: Destabilize spiral and improve Dutch roll damping
Stabilize both spiral and Dutch roll
Destabilize the phugoid and the short period
questions.x: Large |C_lβ| relative to C_nβ rolls the aircraft level in a spiral but couples roll strongly into yaw oscillation, so the designer balances the two.

questions.q: The roll subsidence mode is:
questions.a: A fast first-order roll rate response, damped by C_lp
w: A slow oscillation of roll and yaw together, lightly damped
A long period exchange of speed and altitude
A slow divergence in bank and heading
questions.x: After an aileron input, roll rate settles exponentially with time constant τ = −1/L_p, set by the wing's roll damping.

questions.q: Complete the elevator control power
questions.a: τ_e
w: δ_e
α_t
ε
questions.x: Elevator power grows with tail lift slope, tail efficiency, tail volume, and elevator effectiveness τ_e = dα_t/dδ_e.

questions.q: Match each dynamic mode to its character
pairs: Long period speed-altitude exchange at near-constant α
Fast α and pitch rate oscillation at near-constant V
Slow roll and heading convergence or divergence
questions.x: Two modes are longitudinal and three lateral-directional, the third being roll subsidence.

boards.prompt: Draw me the sustained turn and the P_s constraints on the diagram. Where is the bucket, and what happens when I ask for a higher load factor or a higher altitude?
points: Both come from the master equation with n and P_s = dh_e/dt set by the requirement
The bucket sits at βW/S = (q/n)√(C_D0/K), where parasite and induced terms are equal
Higher n raises the curve and moves the bucket to lower W/S
Higher altitude lowers q and α, which moves the bucket to lower W/S and raises the required T_SL/W_TO
P_s adds the term P_s/V inside the bracket, lifting the whole curve

boards.prompt: Now take this constraint diagram to Mars or Titan. What moves, and which constraints end up driving the design?
points: Stall, landing and takeoff lines scale with ρ and with local g through W
Mars: low density forces very low W/S, large wings, and high C_Lmax
Mars: the low speed of sound caps flight speed through Mach effects at high C_L
Titan: about 4.4 times Earth density and 0.14 g allow high C_L flight at low speed and very low power
Thrust lapse α follows the propulsion type: electric props on both bodies

boards.prompt: Plot maximum rate of climb versus altitude and define the ceilings. Now compare a jet and a piston prop.
points: Rate of climb = (P_A − P_R)/W, maximized at each altitude
Absolute ceiling is where maximum rate of climb reaches zero, with P_A tangent to P_R
Service ceiling is where maximum rate of climb equals 100 ft/min
A jet's P_A = TV rises with speed, so its best climb speed is higher than a prop's
Both P_A curves fall with altitude through the engine lapse, while P_R shifts up and right

boards.prompt: Your engine quits at 10,000 ft. How far can you glide, at what speed, and what changes if you are heavier?
points: tan γ = D/L, so the flattest glide and longest distance occur at (L/D)_max
Distance = h·(L/D)_max in still air, independent of weight
Best glide speed scales with √(W/S), so a heavier aircraft glides the same distance faster and in less time
Minimum sink rate occurs at minimum power, 3C_D0 = KC_L², for maximum time aloft
A headwind shortens ground distance, so pilots add speed above best glide into wind

boards.prompt: Draw the complete V-n diagram for a transport with the flaps envelope and the gust lines. Now tell me where flutter sits.
points: Stall curves n = ±ρV²SC_L/(2W), with the negative side shallower for a cambered wing
Clean limits about +2.5 and −1.0; flaps envelope at +2.0 up to V_F
Gust lines radiate from n = 1 at V = 0, evaluated at V_B, V_C and V_D
The design envelope is the outer boundary of the maneuver and gust envelopes
Flutter clearance extends to 1.15 V_D, outside the envelope

boards.prompt: When do gusts rather than maneuvers set the structural loads, and what happens to that answer as the aircraft burns fuel?
points: Δn = ρ₀U_de V_e a K_g/(2W/S), rising with lift slope and falling with wing loading
Aircraft with low W/S or a high lift slope, such as sailplanes and high aspect ratio transports, are often gust critical
K_g = 0.88μ_g/(5.3 + μ_g) with mass ratio μ_g = 2(W/S)/(ρ c̄ a g), so a lighter aircraft has a smaller K_g and more alleviation
Δn still rises as W/S falls, so the light end of the weight range can set the gust loads

boards.prompt: Draw the real turbofan core cycle on a T-s diagram with component losses. Now add an afterburner.
points: Real compression and expansion slant right with entropy rise, set by η_c and η_t
Burner heat addition follows a slightly falling pressure line from total pressure loss
Turbine work equals compressor and fan work per unit mass, scaled by the mass flows
The afterburner heats along a low pressure isobar after the turbine, raising V_e and thrust
Heat added at low pressure gives poor cycle efficiency, so TSFC rises sharply

boards.prompt: Plot specific thrust and TSFC against bypass ratio and against overall pressure ratio. Then why does a ramjet need no compressor, and what is a turboprop doing differently?
points: Higher bypass ratio lowers specific thrust and lowers TSFC at fixed T_t4
Higher OPR raises thermal efficiency and lowers TSFC, with specific thrust peaking at an intermediate OPR
A ramjet compresses by ram diffusion, τ_r = 1 + (γ−1)M₀²/2, so it needs high flight speed, typically supersonic
A turboprop extracts most of the core energy as shaft power to a propeller, the extreme of high bypass
Propeller tip Mach and blade efficiency limit turboprops to about M 0.6

boards.prompt: Draw a horseshoe vortex for a wing of span b and find the downwash at mid-span. Now turn it into lifting line theory.
points: The horseshoe has a bound vortex along the span and two semi-infinite trailing legs, as Helmholtz requires
Each trailing leg induces Γ/(4πr) in the plane of its end, here with r = b/2
At mid-span the two legs add to w = Γ/(πb), while the bound vortex induces zero on itself
Lifting line superposes infinitely many horseshoes, giving w(y) = (1/4π)∫(dΓ/dη)/(y − η) dη
Elliptic Γ(y) gives uniform downwash, α_i = C_L/(πAR) and C_Di = C_L²/(πAR)

boards.prompt: Why sweep a wing? Now tell me what sweep costs you at low speed and how the area rule fits in.
points: The normal component V cos Λ sets the pressure distribution, raising M_crit and M_dd
Sweep lowers the lift slope and the effective C_Lmax at low speed
Aft sweep drives spanwise boundary layer flow toward the tips, promoting tip stall and pitch up
Fixes include washout, fences, vortilons, and leading edge devices
The area rule shapes the total cross-section distribution smoothly, lowering wave drag near M 1

boards.prompt: Derive rotor thrust with blade element theory and connect it to momentum theory. What does BEMT give you?
points: Blade element: dT = ½ρU²c(C_l cos φ − C_d sin φ) dr per blade with inflow angle φ
Section angle of attack α = θ − φ with φ ≈ v_i/(Ωr)
Momentum theory on an annulus gives dT = 4πρ v_i² r dr in hover
BEMT equates the two to solve for v_i(r), giving thrust, power and figure of merit
Ideal twist θ ∝ 1/r gives uniform inflow and minimum induced power

boards.prompt: What limits a helicopter's top speed? Now the engine fails: walk me through autorotation.
points: Advancing tip Mach (ΩR + V)/a brings drag rise, noise and vibration
Retreating blades at ΩR − V need high α and stall, with reversed flow inboard
These two limits bound advance ratio μ = V/(ΩR) to roughly 0.4 to 0.5
In autorotation upflow through the disk drives the rotor while the aircraft descends
The pilot lowers collective to keep rotor speed, then flares to trade rotor energy for a soft touchdown

boards.prompt: You are sizing a business jet. Build the fuel fraction segment by segment, including reserves. Now the customer adds 10% payload.
points: Warmup and takeoff 0.970, climb 0.985, landing 0.995 from historical data
Cruise from exp(−Rc/(V L/D)) and loiter from exp(−Ec/(L/D))
W_f/W_0 = 1.06(1 − Π segment fractions), with 6% for reserves and trapped fuel
W_0 = (W_crew + W_payload)/(1 − W_f/W_0 − W_e/W_0), iterated since W_e/W_0 depends on W_0
Extra payload grows W_0 by the growth factor, so a 10% payload rise gives a larger rise in W_0

boards.prompt: Derive divergence for a typical section. Now sweep the wing forward, then aft, and tell me what happens.
points: Moment balance K_θθ = q S a e (α₀ + θ) gives θ = qSaeα₀/(K_θ − qSae)
Twist grows without bound at q_D = K_θ/(e a S)
Forward sweep couples bending to nose-up twist at the tip, lowering divergence speed
Aft sweep couples bending to nose-down twist, raising divergence speed and lowering aileron effectiveness
Forward swept designs such as the X-29 used aeroelastically tailored composites to raise q_D

boards.prompt: Write the point-mass equations of motion in wind axes and define every angle.
points: m dV/dt = T cos(α+ε) − D − W sin γ along the velocity
mV dγ/dt = (L + T sin(α+ε)) cos φ − W cos γ normal to the path in the vertical plane
mV cos γ dψ/dt = (L + T sin(α+ε)) sin φ for heading
ε is the installed thrust angle, γ the flight path angle, φ the bank angle, ψ the heading
Steady level flight with small α + ε reduces these to T = D and L = W

boards.prompt: Reduce the equations to a level coordinated turn and derive n, turn rate and radius. Now what limits an instantaneous turn versus a sustained turn?
points: γ = 0 and dγ/dt = 0 give L cos φ = W, so n = 1/cos φ
The heading equation gives ω = g√(n² − 1)/V and R = V²/(g√(n² − 1))
Instantaneous turn is bounded by C_Lmax and the structural limit, peaking at the corner speed
Sustained turn requires T = D at the elevated n, so P_s = 0 sets the limit
Induced drag grows with n², so thrust to weight sets sustained turn performance

boards.prompt: Draw a vertical inside loop and give me the load factor at the top and bottom. Now fly it as an outside loop.
points: Bottom of an inside loop: n = 1 + V²/(gR), the maximum positive load
Top of an inside loop: n = V²/(gR) − 1, with weight helping the turn
An outside loop puts the pilot on the outside of the circle with negative load factors
Bottom of an outside loop, inverted: n = −(1 + V²/(gR)), the most severe negative load
Negative limit loads are smaller in magnitude, so outside loops need large radius or low speed

boards.prompt: Define energy height and specific excess power. Show how P_s links to the master equation and how you would use P_s contours to fly a minimum time climb.
points: h_e = h + V²/(2g) is mechanical energy per unit weight
P_s = (T − D)V/W = dh_e/dt = dh/dt + (V/g)dV/dt
Substituting T = αT_SL, W = βW_TO and dividing by V gives the master equation
P_s contours plotted on an h versus M chart with lines of constant h_e
Minimum time to climb follows the points where P_s contours are tangent to h_e lines

boards.prompt: Build up C_D0 for a transport, component by component. Which numbers dominate?
points: C_D0 = Σ(C_f FF Q S_wet)/S_ref + C_D,misc + C_D,L&P
C_f from Re per component: laminar 1.328/√Re and turbulent 0.455/(log₁₀Re)^2.58
FF rises with thickness ratio for wings and with lower fineness ratio for fuselages
Q captures interference, near 1.0 for faired parts and up to 1.5 for close nacelles
Wing and fuselage carry most of the wetted area, so they dominate parasite drag

boards.prompt: Compare laminar and turbulent skin friction. Now scale the aircraft up by a factor of two in length: what happens to C_D0?
points: Laminar C_f = 1.328/√Re and turbulent C_f = 0.455/(log₁₀Re)^2.58
Turbulent friction is several times larger at the same Re from higher wall shear
Transition depends on Re, pressure gradient, surface finish and sweep
A larger aircraft has higher Re, so C_f falls and C_D0 drops for the same shape
Wetted area ratio S_wet/S_ref is about constant under pure geometric scaling

boards.prompt: Draw C_L versus α for a clean wing, with flaps, and with slats. Explain each device.
points: Trailing edge flaps add camber, shifting α_L0 more negative and raising C_L at each α
Slotted flaps re-energize the boundary layer, and Fowler flaps also add area
Slats delay leading edge stall, extending the lift curve to higher α_stall
Combined slats and multi-slotted flaps give landing C_Lmax near 2.5 to 3.0
Higher C_Lmax lowers stall speed and field length, raising allowed W/S

boards.prompt: Sketch the stall progression on a rectangular, a tapered and a swept wing. How do you fix the bad ones?
points: Rectangular wings stall first at the root, a benign pattern
Tapered wings load the tips and tend to stall outboard
Aft swept wings drive spanwise flow outboard, promoting tip stall and pitch up
Washout, leading edge devices outboard, fences and vortilons move the stall inboard
Root-first stall keeps the ailerons effective and gives a nose-down pitch break

boards.prompt: Draw C_m versus α for a stable aircraft. Define the neutral point and static margin. Now move the CG aft.
points: Stability needs C_mα < 0, and trim at positive α needs C_m0 > 0
The neutral point is the CG location where C_mα = 0
SM = (x_np − x_cg)/c̄, and C_mα = −C_Lα·SM
Moving the CG aft flattens the C_m curve, lowering SM and elevator per g
At the neutral point the slope is zero; aft of it the aircraft needs active control

boards.prompt: How do you set the CG range for an aircraft, and how does tail sizing enter?
points: The forward limit is set by elevator power to trim at C_Lmax and to rotate on takeoff
The aft limit is set by a minimum static margin and acceptable handling
Tail volume V_H = l_t S_t/(c̄ S) sets both the stability contribution and control power
A scissor plot of S_t/S versus x_cg combines both limits to size the tail
Elevator power C_mδe = −a_t η_t V_H τ_e

boards.prompt: Describe the longitudinal dynamic modes. Give me the physics and an approximation for each.
points: Phugoid: long period, lightly damped exchange of speed and altitude at near-constant α
Lanchester approximation: period ≈ π√2·V/g, damping ≈ 1/(√2·L/D)
Short period: fast, well damped α and pitch rate oscillation at near-constant speed
Short period frequency rises with static margin and dynamic pressure
Pilots handle the slow phugoid, while short period characteristics drive handling qualities

boards.prompt: Talk me through lateral-directional stability. What happens with a very large vertical tail versus very large dihedral?
points: C_nβ > 0 from the vertical tail gives directional stability
C_lβ < 0 from dihedral, high wing and aft sweep gives the dihedral effect
Modes: roll subsidence (fast, first order), Dutch roll (yaw-roll oscillation), spiral (slow)
Large C_nβ relative to dihedral effect favors spiral divergence
Large dihedral effect relative to C_nβ favors poorly damped Dutch roll, often fixed with a yaw damper
